character_and_relationship_context:
Sasha Kovalenko is a former history teacher who became a lawyer, and now runs the family firm Kovalenko & Associates in Lviv. Their apartment smells of ink, old paper, and faint menthol from massage gel. Every morning at 7:30, Sasha clears the coffee table, lays out a towel, and stretches their right leg, which is still stiff from a bicycle accident that fractured their femur and bruised their ribs. Physical therapy exercises are on a laminated card, but Sasha has them memorized, just as they once memorized precedent citations. After each repetition, they wait, breathe, and note results in a hardcover ledger with a fountain pen, using columns for date, exercise, repetitions, pain level (1–10), and subjective assessment. Sasha writes 'improved' only when they can flex the ankle an extra degree or stand without gripping the table for a full minute; otherwise they write 'no change' and frown but try again the next day. Their method is patient and methodical, like redlining a stubborn contract clause. By 9 a.m., Sasha reviews client files that a paralegal drops off every Tuesday, despite the doctor's explicit instruction to rest for eight weeks. Sasha worries that junior associates may misplace a statute of limitations or overlook a forged signature, so they review each document, scribbling amendments and running a finger over the type. Anxiety surfaces as a tight jaw when they spot missing notarizations or when the physical therapist calls to ask about overexertion; Sasha sets the phone to silent but keeps it near the files. Sasha came to law late after a decade of teaching history. Their grandfather, a stern, tall man who defended dissidents during Soviet crackdowns, pushed them toward the bar. The trust fund he left is enough to retire, but Sasha never touches the principal, treating it as a sacred obligation to manage for the next generation by purchasing Ukrainian war bonds and reading annual reports with the same scrutiny as liability waivers. Sasha is non-binary, rarely discussed at the firm. They dress in dark blazers and tailored trousers, correct younger colleagues who assume pronouns with patient, legalistic precision, citing the recent gender-recognition court ruling. Sasha still has a slight limp and keeps a carved oak cane from the Carpathians by the door, but refuses to use it except on stairs. The apartment is filled with bookshelves, a desk with a photograph of their grandfather and bronze scales of justice, and a stack of unread novels they plan to start when 'fully healed.' Deep down, they know they will always find a file to open, a clause to reword, or a ledger line to write, because rest is just another problem to solve, and solving problems is the only way they feel in control.

Marta is the upstairs neighbor who brought Sasha a pot of borscht during the first week after the accident and has checked in every few days since, always careful not to push. Sasha appreciates her kindness but knows she tends to linger with small talk after any invitation. They have joined her for brief walks twice before, both times cutting the outing short to return to the ledgers.

Established tendencies: When a physical therapy session is incomplete, Sasha has repeatedly postponed errands, phone calls, and even meals to finish the sequence and write the ledger entry. During earlier recovery weeks, Sasha declined three similar walk invitations from neighbors and colleagues, citing the Tuesday file drop or the therapist's schedule. On rare occasions Sasha accepted an interruption, they returned visibly tense and rewrote the day's assessment entry with extra care.
objective_situation: It is 8:10 a.m., and Sasha is on the living room floor midway through their stretching routine, right leg lifted onto a folded towel. The doorbell rings—it is Marta from upstairs, who knows about the recovery. She is heading to the farmers' market and says she can wait ten minutes if Sasha wants to join her for a slow walk in the sun. The air would be good, and she is ready to leave now. Sasha still needs to finish the remaining repetitions and write today's ledger entry before the Tuesday files arrive at nine. Marta is waiting for an answer.
state_and_available_memories:
Sasha's right quadriceps is mildly aching from the repetitions done so far, and the bruise along the ribs still twinges when they twist. The morning coffee is half-finished and cold on the side table. Sasha has been awake since 6:45, and the anticipation of the Tuesday files has already tightened their jaw slightly.

The doorbell sound reminds Sasha of the morning Marta first came down with the borscht, when Sasha had to pause mid-stretch and ended up forgetting the exact number of repetitions for that day's set. The sun through the living room window cues a memory of the physiotherapist's warning that fresh air helps bone healing, but also that consistency matters more than occasional excursions.
name: Sasha Kovalenko
